title: Domain IV: Procurement Business Principles - Procurement Business Principles - Fair Competition Concepts
subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Which of the following actions best promotes fair and open competition in a public procurement?
options: Specifying a single brand name without an 'or equal' clause.
Using performance specifications instead of restrictive design specifications.
Providing shorter response times to expedite the solicitation process.
Restricting competition strictly to local suppliers.
questions.explain: Performance specifications describe the required outcome rather than how it must be built, allowing multiple vendors to propose innovative solutions, thereby maximizing competition.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: When a public entity must use a brand name specification because of compatibility requirements, what phrase should typically accompany the brand name to maintain competition?
options: No substitutions allowed
Original equipment only
Or approved equal
Proprietary standard
questions.explain: Adding 'or approved equal' or 'or equivalent' to a brand name allows suppliers of comparable products to compete, keeping the procurement process fair.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: What is the primary risk of stringing or splitting purchases?
options: It bypasses competitive bidding thresholds and violates fair competition laws.
It causes unnecessary inventory build-ups.
It forces vendors to submit multiple invoices for a single project.
It requires the use of cooperative contracts.
questions.explain: Splitting purchases divides a large procurement into smaller amounts specifically to circumvent formal competitive bidding thresholds, which is illegal and unethical.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: To ensure an even playing field, how should a procurement officer handle questions received from vendors during the solicitation period?
options: Answer each vendor individually via phone.
Compile all questions and issue a formal written addendum to all prospective bidders.
Ignore questions until the pre-bid conference.
Allow the requesting department to answer vendors directly.
questions.explain: Issuing a formal addendum ensures that all potential respondents receive exactly the same information at the same time, preserving fairness.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: A procurement professional notices that three local vendors seem to be taking turns being the lowest bidder on similar municipal projects. What anti-competitive practice does this suggest?
options: Price fixing
Bid rotation (Bid rigging)
Market allocation
Tie bidding
questions.explain: Bid rotation is a form of bid rigging where colluding firms agree to take turns being the winning bidder to eliminate competition.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Which of the following describes an unbalanced bid?
options: A bid that arrives after the closing date and time.
A bid where line item prices do not reflect reasonable actual costs, shifting the cost heavily to specific items.
A bid where the total price exceeds the agency's budget.
A bid submitted by a vendor who did not attend the mandatory pre-bid meeting.
questions.explain: An mathematically unbalanced bid carries disproportionate pricing on specific line items (e.g., front-loading) which can obscure the true cost and skew competition.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: A late bid is delivered five minutes after the publicly stated deadline due to bad weather. Under standard public procurement practices, what is the most appropriate action?
options: Accept the bid because the delay was caused by an act of God.
Reject the bid and return it unopened to the vendor.
Accept the bid if the pricing is substantially lower than others.
Hold the bid in a secure area and open it only if no other bids are received.
questions.explain: Strict adherence to the published deadline is a cornerstone of fair competition. Accepting a late bid provides an unfair advantage and violates standard procurement laws.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Requiring a vendor to have exactly 20 years of experience to bid on standard landscaping services is generally considered:
options: A best practice to ensure quality.
An unduly restrictive specification.
A required element of performance specifications.
A standard bonding requirement.
questions.explain: Excessive experience requirements for standard services arbitrarily limit competition without serving a legitimate operational need, making them unduly restrictive.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: What is the primary justification for conducting a sole source procurement?
options: The end user prefers to work with a specific vendor.
There is only one known capable supplier of the required goods or services.
The required goods are available locally.
The agency needs to spend remaining budget funds quickly before year-end.
questions.explain: A sole source procurement is only justified when market research indicates that the required commodity or service is available from strictly one vendor.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: When establishing evaluation criteria for a Request for Proposals (RFP), when should the criteria be developed and finalized?
options: After proposals are received but before they are opened.
During the evaluation committee's initial review of the proposals.
Before the solicitation is issued to the public.
After the vendor shortlist has been created.
questions.explain: To ensure fairness and transparency, evaluation criteria and their weights must be established before the RFP is released and clearly communicated in the solicitation documents.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: A bidder submits a proposal indicating they will perform the work but modifies the agency's mandatory insurance limits. This bid should typically be deemed:
options: Non-responsible
Non-responsive
Collusive
Acceptable, pending negotiation
questions.explain: A bid is 'non-responsive' if it fails to conform to the essential, mandatory requirements (such as insurance limits) outlined in the invitation for bids.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: In a formal competitive bidding process, two responsive and responsible bidders submit the exact same low price. How is this typically resolved?
options: The contract is split evenly between both bidders.
The bids are rejected, and the solicitation is re-issued.
It is resolved according to the agency's tie-breaker policy, such as a coin toss or local preference.
The procurement officer negotiates with both to get a lower price.
questions.explain: In competitive sealed bidding (IFB), negotiation is not permitted. Tie bids are resolved by predefined statutory or policy mechanisms, such as a coin toss or applying a preference.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: What does a 'pre-bid conference' achieve in relation to fair competition?
options: It allows the agency to eliminate unfavorable vendors early.
It provides a forum to clarify specifications equally to all interested bidders.
It replaces the need for issuing written addenda.
It locks in preliminary pricing.
questions.explain: Pre-bid conferences allow the agency to explain complex requirements and answer questions in an open forum, ensuring all potential bidders share the same understanding.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: Which condition constitutes a valid 'single-source' procurement (as opposed to a sole source)?
options: Only one vendor makes the product.
Multiple vendors exist, but the agency chooses to buy from one specific vendor for standardization or specific business reasons.
A vendor holds the exclusive patent to a product.
The procurement requires an emergency response.
questions.explain: Single-source implies that while competition exists in the market, the agency has justified directing the purchase to one vendor (often for standardization or compatibility), unlike sole source where only one vendor exists.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles

questions.q: A conflict of interest in public procurement directly threatens fair competition because:
options: It compromises the objectivity of the evaluation, giving an unfair advantage to a specific vendor.
It forces vendors to offer lower prices.
It delays the public notice period.
It requires the use of multi-step bidding.
questions.explain: Conflicts of interest undermine the impartiality of the process, potentially favoring one entity and directly negating fair and open competition.
questions.subject: Procurement Business Principles
